nameStory: Elakatothrix gelatinosa doesn't have a widely recognized common name since it's a microscopic freshwater alga that most people never notice. The scientific name comes from Greek 'elakatos' meaning 'small' and 'thrix' meaning 'hair,' referring to its thread-like appearance, while 'gelatinosa' describes the jelly-like substance that surrounds these tiny organisms.
description: This is actually a microscopic green alga, not a traditional plant that you'd spot while hiking! Elakatothrix gelatinosa forms tiny, hair-like threads made up of single cells lined up in a row, all surrounded by a clear, jelly-like coating. Individual cells are incredibly small - you'd need a microscope to see them clearly - but sometimes they form visible green films or mats in very still, clean freshwater. The whole colony might look like a thin green scum or delicate green threads floating in the water.

idTips.label: Microscopic Structure
idTips.description: Cells form thread-like chains (called filaments) that are surrounded by a clear, gelatinous sheath that feels slippery if you can collect enough to touch

idTips.label: Water Appearance
idTips.description: Creates thin green films or mats on very still water surfaces that look almost like green silk threads floating

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Any visible growth feels extremely slippery and mucilaginous (jelly-like) due to the gelatinous coating around the cell chains

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when healthy and getting good light, but may appear yellowish-green in shaded or nutrient-poor conditions

habitat: Found in very clean, still freshwater environments like pristine ponds, quiet stream pools, and sometimes temporary puddles in rocky areas. Prefers cool, well-oxygenated water with low nutrient levels, often in woodland settings or high-elevation areas where water quality remains excellent.

seasonality.spring: Most active growth period as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Look for thin green films starting to appear on pond surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when visible mats or films are most likely to be spotted on still water surfaces in shaded areas.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows but may still be visible in protected areas. Often persists longer in consistently cool water.
seasonality.winter: Generally dormant or present only as resistant cells. Unlikely to form visible growth in frozen conditions.

funFact: Despite being microscopic, this tiny alga is incredibly important for water quality - its presence often indicates that a body of water is exceptionally clean and healthy, making it a living indicator of pristine aquatic ecosystems!
confusionNotes: Most people would confuse any visible growth with pond scum or other algae, but unlike the thick, smelly blue-green algae blooms, Elakatothrix forms delicate, odorless films and actually indicates clean water rather than polluted conditions.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of those organisms that highlights how much microscopic life exists around us that we never notice. While called an 'alga,' it's quite different from seaweeds - it's a single-celled freshwater organism that just happens to be green and photosynthetic like plants.
compareHints: **Note: Information about relatives is uncertain due to limited data.** This appears to be the only Elakatothrix species commonly found in New England waters. It differs from other thread-like freshwater algae by its distinctive gelatinous sheath and preference for very clean water conditions, unlike many algae that thrive in nutrient-rich environments.
